info:
This period sits at the opening of the Holocene Climatic Optimum, which would eventually bring maximum average temperatures of 1–2°C above today's. The second sea-level acceleration pulse, briefly exceeding a metre per century, fell within this window.

In the Baltic basin, the Ancylus Lake gave way around 7550 BCE to the brackish Littorina Sea, close to the basin's modern configuration, though its salinity history remained complex for millennia.

Doggerland was now significantly reduced, its final remnants , a mosaic of reed marsh, alder carr, open water and islands, soon to disappear beneath the rising North Sea entirely.
background: The most structurally forested period yet — oak and elm dominated the canopy across much of the map, with lime advancing through the warmest and most oceanic western areas and alder colonising river valleys and wet ground rapidly. Alder carr became a defining feature of floodplains and coastal lowlands, including the margins of the shrinking North Sea land bridge. This is the Mesolithic climax — the period when the hunter-gatherer populations of northwest Europe reached their greatest density and ecological sophistication, living in a landscape that was predominantly forested but structured by their own burning and hunting practices. Structurally this forest was denser than the Eemian natural baseline — a consequence of megafauna loss rather than a natural climax state. Perhaps 15–25% fully open ground remained, concentrated along coasts, wetlands and actively managed zones. Doggerland was by now significantly reduced by rising sea levels, its final remnants likely a mosaic of reed marsh, alder carr and open water.
floraDescription:
Europe's forests continued to diversify as oak, elm and hazel became widespread across much of the continent. Lime gradually expanded into warmer regions, while alder established dense woodlands along rivers, lakes and wetlands.

The increasingly complex forest structure created a rich variety of habitats, although the closing canopy reduced many of the sun-loving grasses and flowering plants that had flourished in earlier periods. Natural disturbances, browsing by large mammals and occasional Mesolithic fires maintained scattered clearings within an otherwise continuous woodland.

By the end of the Boreal, Europe supported mature mixed forests unlike anything seen since before the last Ice Age, setting the stage for the continent's climatic optimum.
faunaDescription:
By the Late Boreal, Europe's dense forests covered much of the landscape. Large herbivores continued to shape the woodlands, rivers flowed freely across broad floodplains and wetlands supported a rich bopdiversity of birds and fish.

Brown bears, wolves and lynx still roamed widely, while beavers helped to engineer dynamic freshwater habitats throughout the continent.

The first farming communities were beginning to emerge in southeastern Europe, while most of northern and western Europe remained occupied by hunter-gatherers. By this time, Europe's ecosystems were missing many of the giant herbivores that had once maintained a more open and species-rich landscape.
